newsitem.title: USA: Health advocates push Alaska tobacco tax hike.
newsitem.headline: Health advocates push Alaska tobacco tax hike.

text.p: Alaska health advocates said Thursday they were optimistic about a renewed campaign to raise cigarette taxes in the state by $1 a pack.

The tax hike, aimed at discouraging teenage smoking while helping to replace dwindling oil revenues, was blocked by the state legislature this year, but it has a better chance of success next year, advocates said at a health conference.
"I think this battle is not over and a year from now we'll be telling a quite different story," Anne Marie Holen of the Alaska Native Health Board said.

If state lawmakers pass the increase, which Gov. Tony Knowles plans to reintroduce in January, it would give Alaska the nation's highest tobacco tax at $1.29 a pack, surpassing Washington state's 82.5 cents. Health advocates say the high tax is appropriate for a state with one of the nation's highest teenage smoking and tobacco-chewing rates.
It also would create a model for other states, said Michael Eriksen, director of the Office on Smoking and Health at the U.S. Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
"If Alaska does increase the excise tax by $1 or more, that would have a dramatic effect on the rest of the country," Eriksen said at the conference.
Advocates meeting at the three-day Alaska Health Summit said the tax hike would discourage about a third of the children who currently take up smoking or tobacco chewing.

The tax increase cleared the Republican-controlled state Senate by a 17-3 margin in May but was blocked by Republican House Speaker Gail Phillips, who said the measure would go against her "no new taxes" pledge.
But with public opinion polls showing three-quarters of Alaskans endorsing the measure, even Phillips now favours it, albeit at a reduced level.

Alaska has unique circumstances that would make a large tobacco tax successful, health advocates said. For one thing, the state is facing a budget crunch from declining production at the giant Prudhoe Bay oil field and needs to find other sources of government revenue. The tobacco tax increase would produce about $42 million annually.

The state is also isolated from potential sources of smuggled cigarettes, they said. Tobacco is more expensive in Canada's Yukon Territory and British Columbia province, the only regions sharing a land border with Alaska.

Eriksen said a $1-a-pack increase would not be as dramatic as some opponents claim. In 1964, the year the Surgeon General mandated health warnings on cigarette packages, taxes accounted for 50 percent of cigarette prices. Now they account for only 30 percent of the retail price, he said.
"A $1 tax increase would rectify that," he said. "It's really appropriate. It's just that no other state has had the courage to take it on."
